# Public Evidence Chain: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Software Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive assessment

The public evidence supports a specific cascading-compromise sequence:

1. A 3CX employee’s computer was compromised through a trojanized installer for Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER application.
2. The intruders used that foothold to move through the 3CX environment and compromise both Windows and macOS build systems.
3. Malicious code was inserted into legitimate, digitally signed 3CX DesktopApp installers.
4. Customers who downloaded affected 3CX DesktopApp versions received software containing a first-stage downloader and, in selected cases, additional payloads.
5. The campaign was publicly associated with a North Korea-linked activity cluster. Mandiant tracked the operation as **UNC4736**, assessed it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster, and gave its relationship to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity a **moderate-confidence** assessment. Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram deployment to **Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence**, while MITRE ATT&CK records AppleJeus as malware used by Lazarus Group. The evidence therefore supports a North Korean/Lazarus-associated attribution, but the exact organizational identity should not be stated as certain.

The strongest reconstruction comes from Mandiant’s incident-response findings because it directly addresses the intrusion path into 3CX’s environment and identifies the prior Trading Technologies compromise. Contemporary reporting from Cybersecurity Dive, Kaspersky, Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency, and WIRED corroborates the nature, scale, victimology, and public attribution of the campaign.

## Source identification

To avoid ambiguity, the supplied sources are identified as follows:

| Source ID | Source | Principal evidentiary contribution |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Cybersecurity Dive, March 30, 2023 | Initial public reporting, affected versions and scope, suspected North Korea-linked activity |
| S2 | WIRED, April 3, 2023 | Early victimology and Gopuram targeting of cryptocurrency firms |
| S3 | Mandiant/Google Cloud, April 20, 2023 | Initial intrusion vector, build-environment compromise, malware chain, UNC4736 assessment |
| S4 | Kaspersky Securelist, April 3, 2023 | Gopuram deployment, targeted cryptocurrency victims, Lazarus assessment |
| S5 | Google Threat Analysis Group, March 24, 2022 | Prior AppleJeus activity, Trading Technologies compromise, North Korean cryptocurrency targeting |
| S6 | MITRE ATT&CK Software S0584 | AppleJeus description and association with Lazarus Group |
| S7 | MITRE ATT&CK Group G0032 | Lazarus Group identity, aliases, and attribution caveats |
| S8 | Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, March 31, 2023 | Affected 3CX versions, capabilities, and defensive advice |
| S9 | WIRED, April 20, 2023 | Public explanation of the cascading, two-stage supply-chain compromise |

The supplied material contains duplicate copies of several URLs. Each URL is treated as one source and cited once in the reference list.

## Incident scope and initial discovery

The 3CX DesktopApp is enterprise communications software providing voice, video-conferencing, chat, and call-management functionality. Contemporary reporting stated that 3CX claimed more than 600,000 corporate customers and more than 12 million daily active users. Huntress reportedly identified more than 242,000 publicly exposed 3CX phone-management systems and sent 2,595 incident reports involving a malicious 3CXDesktopApp.exe hash signed by 3CX on March 13, 2023. These figures describe potential exposure and observed indicators, not confirmed compromise of every organization counted. ([Jones, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/) [S1])

CrowdStrike reported unexpected malicious behavior from a legitimate, signed 3CX binary beginning in late March 2023. The observed behavior included beaconing to attacker-controlled infrastructure, deployment of second-stage payloads, and, in a small number of cases, hands-on-keyboard activity. CrowdStrike initially observed activity on Windows and macOS, although the supplied reporting notes that other researchers had not independently confirmed the macOS activity at that point. ([Jones, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/) [S1])

The Singapore Cyber Security Agency identified the following affected versions:

| Platform | Affected versions reported by CSA |
|---|---|
| Windows Electron application | 18.12.407 and 18.12.416 |
| macOS Electron application | 18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416 |

CSA stated that the trojanized application could harvest system information and steal data and stored credentials from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox profiles. ([Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, 2023](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/) [S8])

## Reconstruction of the public evidence chain

### Stage 1: Prior compromise of Trading Technologies software

Mandiant identified the initial compromise of 3CX’s network as a malicious software package downloaded from the Trading Technologies website. The package was a tampered installer for **X_TRADER**, a Trading Technologies application that remained available for download even though the platform had reportedly been discontinued in 2020. Mandiant identified the installer as `X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe` with MD5 hash `ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3])

The X_TRADER installer was digitally signed with a certificate whose subject was “Trading Technologies International, Inc.” It contained a signed `Setup.exe`, which dropped two malicious DLLs and a benign executable. The benign executable was used to side-load one of the malicious DLLs. The resulting loading process used SIGFLIP and DAVESHELL to decrypt and execute a modular backdoor named **VEILEDSIGNAL**. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3])

Mandiant’s technical comparison identified several similarities between the compromised X_TRADER and 3CX applications:

- The same RC4 key, `3jB(2bsG#@c7`, was used in SIGFLIP configurations.
- Both relied on SIGFLIP, a tool capable of modifying signed PE files without invalidating their signatures.
- Both used DAVESHELL for reflective, in-memory loading.
- Both used the hard-coded cookie variable `__tutma`.
- Both encrypted data with AES-256-GCM.

These overlaps are important because they link the earlier Trading Technologies compromise to the later 3CX compromise through shared tooling and implementation characteristics, rather than merely through broad similarities such as the use of DLLs. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3])

### Stage 2: Entry into the 3CX corporate environment

Mandiant’s reconstruction states that the malicious X_TRADER package was installed on a 3CX employee’s computer. The compromise gave the threat actor access to the 3CX environment. The attacker then harvested credentials and moved laterally through the organization. WIRED summarized Mandiant’s findings as showing that the X_TRADER foothold enabled access to the 3CX network, including a server used for software development. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]; [Greenberg, 2023b](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two) [S9])

Mandiant also identified a compiled version of the open-source **Fast Reverse Proxy** project in the environment. The file was named `MsMpEng.exe`, had MD5 hash `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`, and was dropped in `C:\Windows\System32`. Mandiant described the tool as being used for lateral movement within the 3CX organization. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3])

### Stage 3: Compromise of the build environment

The attacker eventually compromised both the Windows and macOS build environments used by 3CX.

On the Windows build environment, Mandiant identified:

- **TAXHAUL**, a launcher that decrypted shellcode stored in a Windows registry-transaction file path.
- **COLDCAT**, a downloader that generated a host identifier and communicated with command-and-control infrastructure.
- Persistence through DLL search-order hijacking involving the IKEEXT service.
- Execution with LocalSystem privileges.

On the macOS build server, Mandiant identified **POOLRAT**, a macOS backdoor using Launch Daemons for persistence. Mandiant clarified that a sample previously described in some reporting as a new malware family was, in its assessment, POOLRAT. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3])

This stage is the decisive link between the initial employee compromise and the mass distribution event. The attackers did not merely compromise an endpoint that happened to run 3CX software; they reached the systems used to build or package the software. That access allowed them to insert malicious components into a legitimate 3CX release.

### Stage 4: Trojanized 3CX distribution

Mandiant reported that affected 3CX DesktopApp version 18.12.416 and earlier contained malicious code. The compromised application ran a downloader called **SUDDENICON**. SUDDENICON retrieved additional command-and-control server information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. The decrypted infrastructure was then used to download **ICONICSTEALER**, a data-mining component that collected browser information. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3])

Kaspersky independently described a similar chain: a malicious DLL in the installer decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`; the payload extracted command-and-control URLs from icons hosted in a GitHub repository; the resulting infostealer collected system information and browser history. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4])

The malicious application was particularly difficult to detect because it was distributed as legitimate 3CX software and carried a valid 3CX signature. Researchers also identified DLL side-loading as a key execution technique. ([Jones, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/) [S1]; [Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, 2023](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/) [S8])

## Selective targeting and final payloads

The campaign appears to have used a broad initial distribution stage followed by selective victim filtering. Kaspersky observed the full Gopuram backdoor on fewer than ten machines in its telemetry and reported that the affected organizations appeared to include cryptocurrency companies, especially in Western Asia. Kaspersky described this as “surgical precision,” but the supplied evidence does not establish that cryptocurrency companies were the only targets or that cryptocurrency theft was successfully completed. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4]; [Greenberg, 2023a](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/) [S2])

Kaspersky identified Gopuram components including:

- `wlbsctrl.dll`, MD5 `9f85a07d4b4abff82ca18d990f062a84`;
- An encrypted shellcode payload stored under `C:\Windows\System32\config\TxR\`;
- `guard64.dll` as the main Gopuram module;
- Additional modules for registry, services, timestomping, process injection, networking, and other functions.

The `wlbsctrl.dll` component was loaded through IKEEXT-related DLL hijacking and decrypted the shellcode using `CryptUnprotectData`. Gopuram could interact with the file system, create processes, and launch in-memory modules. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4])

## Public attribution

### Mandiant and UNC4736

Mandiant tracked the activity as **UNC4736**, describing it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean **AppleJeus** activity. It also noted overlap with multiple North Korean operators and weaker infrastructure overlap with suspected APT43-related clusters. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3])

Mandiant’s attribution was based on several linked observations:

- Shared tooling and code between the Trading Technologies and 3CX compromises.
- The connection between POOLRAT in the 3CX environment and an older POOLRAT sample associated with the AppleJeus operation.
- Infrastructure overlap involving cryptocurrency-focused campaigns.
- Prior Google TAG reporting on the compromise of `tradingtechnologies[.]com` and North Korean activity targeting cryptocurrency and fintech organizations.

### Kaspersky and Lazarus

Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram deployment to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence. Its reasoning included Gopuram’s coexistence with AppleJeus on a prior cryptocurrency-company victim, shared infrastructure, use of domains previously associated with Lazarus, and the alignment between cryptocurrency targeting and Lazarus activity. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4])

MITRE ATT&CK describes AppleJeus as a malware family used by Lazarus Group against cryptocurrency and other sectors. It lists Lazarus Group as the group associated with AppleJeus. ([MITRE ATT&CK, 2025](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/) [S6]) MITRE also cautions that “Lazarus Group” is often used as an umbrella designation for multiple North Korean operators and that shared personnel, infrastructure, malware, and tradecraft can make precise attribution difficult. ([MITRE ATT&CK, 2026](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/) [S7])

The appropriate conclusion is therefore:

> The 3CX compromise was publicly attributed to a North Korea-linked operation, tracked by Mandiant as UNC4736 and associated by Mandiant and Kaspersky with financially motivated AppleJeus/Lazarus activity. The available evidence supports that assessment, but it does not justify treating “Lazarus,” “UNC4736,” and every other North Korean alias as proven interchangeable identities.

## Contradictions and unresolved issues

Several differences in the reporting should be preserved rather than silently reconciled.

| Issue | Evidence conflict or limitation | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Exact actor identity | Mandiant used UNC4736 and gave a moderate-confidence AppleJeus relationship; Kaspersky gave a medium-to-high-confidence Lazarus assessment; other reporting used different North Korean labels. | North Korean nexus is stronger than any exact subgroup identification. |
| Victim scope | 3CX had hundreds of thousands of potentially exposed users, but Kaspersky observed Gopuram on fewer than ten machines. | Initial exposure was broad; confirmed high-value second-stage targeting was narrow in available telemetry. |
| Cryptocurrency objective | Kaspersky and WIRED identified cryptocurrency firms as apparent targets, but Kaspersky reported no evidence of completed cryptocurrency theft in the observed victims. | Cryptocurrency targeting is supported; successful theft is not established by these sources. |
| macOS activity | CrowdStrike reported Windows and macOS activity, while the Cybersecurity Dive account noted that other researchers had not confirmed macOS activity at that time. | macOS compromise was reported, but contemporaneous independent confirmation was incomplete. |
| “First” cascading supply-chain attack | Mandiant described this as the first such incident it had seen and the first known concrete example; this is an evidentiary claim, not proof that no earlier case existed. | The 3CX–Trading Technologies chain is the first documented example identified by Mandiant in the supplied sources. |

## Conclusion

The public evidence establishes a coherent chain from an earlier software supply-chain compromise to the 3CX incident. The attackers first compromised a Trading Technologies X_TRADER installer, used the resulting access on a 3CX employee’s computer, harvested credentials, moved laterally, compromised 3CX’s Windows and macOS build environments, and inserted malicious components into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp releases. The releases then distributed a downloader and browser-information stealer broadly, while a modular Gopuram backdoor was deployed selectively against a small number of apparent high-value victims.

My assessment is that the most defensible attribution is **a North Korea-linked, financially motivated operation associated with AppleJeus and Lazarus-related activity, tracked by Mandiant as UNC4736**. “Lazarus” is a reasonable public attribution label for the campaign’s Gopuram activity, but UNC4736 should remain the more precise analytic designation for the 3CX operation itself because Mandiant’s evidence expresses the relationship to Lazarus-associated activity as an assessment rather than an absolute identification.
